structured_output.hypothesis: In sunflower capitula the clockwise and anticlockwise parastichies cross at an approximately constant angle along their length (isogonal), and that angle is only rarely close to 90 degrees.
structured_output.pass_criterion: Both conditions hold on at least 100 analysed heads with clearly regular lattices. (1) Isogonality: the median within-head standard deviation of the local crossing angle, measured in three radial annuli (0.3-0.5R, 0.5-0.7R, 0.7-0.9R, where R is the capitulum radius), is below 10 degrees, and the median absolute difference between the outer and middle annulus mean angles is below 10 degrees. (2) Orthogonality infrequent: fewer than 25% of heads have a head-mean crossing angle within 90 +/- 5 degrees.
structured_output.fail_criterion: The claim is refuted if either (a) the median within-head SD of crossing angle across annuli is 15 degrees or more, or the median outer-vs-middle annulus difference is 15 degrees or more (angle is not constant), or (b) 50% or more of heads have a head-mean crossing angle within 90 +/- 5 degrees (orthogonality is the common case). Results between the pass and fail thresholds on either condition count as inconclusive.
structured_output.interpretation: Thompson's 'spirals intersect isogonally' means the two families of parastichy curves (the visible clockwise and anticlockwise spirals, e.g. 34 and 55) cross at one constant angle, as logarithmic spirals about a common pole do. 'Orthogonal intersection' (Church's view) means a 90 degree crossing. It is measured as the angle between the tangent directions of the two parastichy families at each seed, estimated from seed or parastichy positions digitised from the annotated capitulum photographs. Modern note: lattice theory (golden-angle packing) predicts the crossing angle approaches 90 degrees at large radius in regular heads, so condition (2) may well fail. The test is of Thompson's statement as written, with the thresholds fixed in advance. The dataset provides images and parastichy annotations, not ready-made coordinates, so seed centres must be extracted first.

dataset.name: Data from: Novel Fibonacci and non-Fibonacci structure in the sunflower: results of a citizen science experiment
dataset.publisher: Dryad (data from Swinton et al., Royal Society Open Science 2016)
dataset.why_it_fits: Public Dryad record from a citizen-science study of sunflower capitula. It includes annotated seedhead images (zip file) and recorded clockwise and anticlockwise parastichy numbers. Fields to use: the annotated seedhead images (to digitise seed positions and fit parastichy tangents for crossing angles by annulus) and the parastichy-number table (to select regular heads with an assignable parastichy pair). I did not confirm that per-seed coordinates are included, so seed positions will probably need extracting from the images.
